posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
Here's the artist's site. Unfortunately there is no text describing what's going on. Stylusart has a bit more.

It looks like a bunch of wide web rainbow foil wrapped around the building. Could be quite cool to behold!

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: Ed, is wide web still only 6 inches? We were doing that about 20 years ago. I take this from an estimation of size from the first photo with the gentleman's hand close to the foil where you can see the "square" webbing.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
Wide web is up to 40" width and 40" repeat. We were spinning 45" by 45" plates when I worked at CFC.

There are other places that are doing similar sizes, like ITW, Wavefront, and who knows what is going on in the Far East.

posts.author: edelbrp
posts.content_md:

-Phil

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Ed, did you see the photo of the gentleman close to the material? It looks to be small, about 6 or so inches.

So you mean there are actually embossed holograms out there printing a single image 40" wide? That's great!

Our biggest hurdle then was not the embosser but the nickel plating process, at the time the larger the resist the more uneven the shims, thus a differential in pressure where it was thicker and thinner when placed in the embosser. Hey, I guess the industry has grow. Man, I wish I was still in the field. I would do anything, short of compimising my income (family now) to work in that field again.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md: No, you don't. It's a cutthroat business dominated by mean and stupid people. The pinheads at CFC eliminated my position to save a few bucks to make themselves look better for potential buyers of the company. Plus there was a definite lack of holo jobs coming in, possibly because nobody wants holography or more than likely because their sales force is less than inept. Their stock is at an all time high, not because of holography but because they lucked into a position of being the major US supplier of wood grain films, another of their product lines, only because their competition closed down their Philly plant.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:a5c7a923c2="Ed Wesley"]It's a cutthroat business dominated by mean and stupid people. [/quote:a5c7a923c2]

You forgot "ignorant". I've had to cringe when I've heard management glorify the possibilities of holography to customers. I too have been in trouble in several jobs because the Powers That Be don't seem to want to know that what they is probably not true. Unfortunately this sort of thing proagates within the holographic community. From:

"If you break up a hologram, every piece of the broken hologram contains the entire image" (I just recently was asked to make an 11"x13" hologram of a 2D image for a customer who had heard this and wanted to cut up the holo and pass on "the entire hologram" from every small piece)

to:

"If you make a hologram of a bowl of water and focus a microscope on the image, you can see holographic bacteria."

Amazing, this microscope! Automatically negates all dispersion and aberration while subtending a tiny angle in such a tiny image field! 

By the way, Hans told us at the SPIE Holography Group Meeting this year, that even the security industry is hurting. Their Holy Grails, bank notes and credit cards, are apparently no longer considered secure. Credit cards are veering away from holograms to other image technologies. I see a fresnel zone plate on the new American Express cards.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> that even the security industry is hurting.

If it can't be copied, it's secure but useless as a product. If it can be copied, it's not secure!

It was only a matter of time before those facts came back to bite them in the butt.
